articles.title: Mãe de Tabata Amaral sofre acidente durante agenda de campanha e está internada na UTI | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a candidata a deputada federal, Reni Amaral bateu a cabeça no chão no sábado (3), no Parque da Independência, em São Paulo, em uma agenda de campanha; ela passou por cirurgia de emergência.
articles.summary: Segundo a candidata a deputada federal, Reni Amaral bateu a cabeça no chão no sábado (3), no Parque da Independência, em São Paulo,  em uma agenda de campanha; ela passou por cirurgia de emergência.
articles.body:
Deputada federal Tabata Amaral (PSB-SP) — Foto: Vinicius Loures/Câmara dos Deputados

A mãe da candidata a deputada federal Tabata Amaral (PSB), Reni Amaral, está internada na Unidade de Terapia Intensiva (UTI) do Hospital São Camilo, em São Paulo , após sofrer um acidente durante uma agenda de campanha da filha neste sábado (3).

Segundo Tabata, a mãe a acompanhava em uma atividade no Parque da Independência, na Zona Sul da capital paulista, quando sofreu o acidente e bateu a cabeça no chão.

Reni foi levada ao Hospital São Camilo, onde passou por uma cirurgia de emergência. Neste domingo (4), ela permanecia internada na UTI, em estado estável, porém grave, de acordo com a candidata.

Em publicação nas redes sociais, Tabata agradeceu à equipe do hospital e ao médico Fernando Gomes, que acompanha o atendimento da mãe. Ela também informou que novos exames serão realizados para avaliar a evolução do quadro após a cirurgia.

“Peço, de coração, que vocês mantenham minha mãe em suas orações”, escreveu a candidata.

articles.title: West in Pictures: Birnbeck Pier in cardboard and misty mornings
articles.summary: Our weekly round-up of photographs from across the West.
articles.body:
Work took place on two piers - albeit, only one which was real - in Weston-super-Mare this week.

Congratulations are in order for one man in Gloucestershire who grew a world record-breaking giant cucumber.

And the first signs of autumn are starting to show across the county as we enter the final few months of the year.

Here's a round-up of some of the best photographs from across the West this week.

The red wall: Finished in time for this season, there is a new mural towering over Bristol City fans as they walk the final few yards to Ashton Gate for home games. Co-ordinated by art4fans.uk, it evokes defensive heroes of the club's past and was made by local artists Inkie and Jody, among others.

Cooking up a storm: FŌDA, a "Festival of Food Ideas", brought together independent food and drink producers and gave youngsters a chance to try their hand at cooking. It was headed up by Josh Eggleton from the Pony Chew Valley, with Team Canteen.

Picture pier-fect: A giant cardboard pier - based on Birnbeck Pier, which can be seen in the background - was created by hundreds of volunteers using 2,000 boxes and 23.6 miles of sticky tape. It eventually fell victim to strong coastal winds and was squashed and recycled.

Play on: Classical music fans gathered at the Bristol Beacon on Thursday night as the Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra launched its performance cycle of Beethoven's Symphonies, under the title Road to Joy!

Good progress: Restoration work is well under way on Birnbeck Pier. A quarter of the Grade II* listed structure is now complete, with the remainder of the project on course to be completed by next year.

Time to play: The National Padel Championships took place in Bristol this week and brought together the country's leading players as they competed against each other for the coveted title.

Record-breaking: Graham Barratt from Gloucestershire won in the longest cucumber category at the National Giant Vegetables Championship with a plant measuring a whopping 7.598m (24.6 feet).

Gameday: Gloucester fans who headed to Kingsholm on Saturday were rewarded by an emphatic win - a 48-0 thumping of Harlequins.

Misty morning: Signs of autumn are starting to appear, with more misty mornings - like this one captured by Weather Watcher Cotswold Bob - inevitably on the way.

Preparing for take-off: The US air force's planes carried on taking off from RAF Fairford as a major incident was declared and a major counter-terrorism probe was launched.

The end of an era: A final evening of events was held on Thursday at Dowty Sports and Social Club in Gloucester before the venue closed its doors for the final time after 66 years.

Huge win: Kate Daven-Thomas, who works at a florist in Minehead, won £300,000 on a National Lottery Cashword Extra Scratchcard.

Golden Glastonbury: There were more foggy scenes across Somerset too this week, with Glastonbury Tor peeking up in the sky in front of the sunrise.

Reservoir run: More than 200 amateur runners took part in a run beside Chew Valley Lake to raise money for Bristol Children's Hospital.

Baaa-sking in the sun: Weather Watcher Nutkin captured a shot of these woolly sheep wandering on a hillside in Somerset

Love at first spike: Keepers introduced porcupines Gus and Pumpkin to each other at Longleat earlier this week. It is hoped the pair will bring porcupettes to the park in the future.

Stunning: Getty photographer Finnbarr Webster took this lovely picture of the west front of Salisbury Cathedral as the sun was setting earlier this week.

On your marks: Callum Hutchinson riding Gran Dia (blue) won The Salisbury Annual Badgeholders "Bluestocking" British EBF Novice Stakes at Salisbury Racecourse on Thursday.

Time for a refresh: The Millenium White Horse in the Roundway Down area of Devizes is being re-chalked by a group of volunteers.

Moments of Light: Dorothy House is celebrating its 50th anniversary with a special light installation created by artist Bruce Munro. The charity said it was "a space for reflection, remembrance and connection".

Follow BBC Bristol on Facebook , X and Instagram . Send your story ideas to us on email or via WhatsApp on 0800 313 4630 .

articles.title: Mold could be lurking in your coffee maker as expert reveals 5 ways to keep it clean
articles.summary: A two-time U.S. Barista Champion debunks fears about coffee mold for home brews — and shares five tips for better brewing and coffee maker cleaning.
articles.body: Brewing a cup of morning coffee is an essential part of most Americans’ routines — but cleaning the coffee maker isn’t, a lot of the time. Recent reports and viral social media posts have highlighted the potential for mold and bacteria to build up inside home coffee makers — while beans marketed as tested for mold have left some drinkers wondering what may be lurking beyond the carafe. But Heather Perry, the California-based CEO of Klatch Coffee and a two-time U.S. Barista Champion, said there is little reason for most home brewers to panic. COFFEE LOVERS CAN TAKE HEART: UP TO 5 CUPS A DAY APPEARS SAFE FOR MOST ADULTS, EXPERTS SAY She said a few simple steps can ensure a better cup. "Coffee equipment cleanliness has way more importance when it comes to the flavor and the way it impacts it than [as] a true safety issue," Perry told Fox News Digital. "Coffee is totally fine to be type B about." She debunked common coffee fears and shared five tips for a better brew. 1. Mold fears should not make you panic Recent warnings have made coffee-cleaning and sourcing issues sound more alarming than they need to be, said Perry. COFFEE EXPERT WARNS ONE LAZY HABIT CAN TURN YOUR SINGLE-SERVE MACHINE INTO A GERM TRAP "You do not at all need to be worried at home about mold and bacteria," Perry told Fox News Digital. "It is incredibly low on the list of things to worry about, in my opinion, when it comes to coffee equipment." As for coffee being branded as "tested for mold," Perry had a blunt assessment. "That is 100% a marketing thing," she said. 2. Carafe needs more attention than the reservoir The part you should be most worried about cleaning is the pot, Perry said — which can throw off the taste of your cup. "Once that’s in your pot, you’re gonna taste that in your cups," she said. 'HOTEL VIBES' COFFEE HACK RAISES EYEBROWS AS EXPERTS WARN OF SLEEP QUALITY RISKS Coffee stains can especially build up in insulated carafes that can't be seen. "Those thermos pots are where I think we find a lot of coffee stains are staying, and that will absolutely begin to affect the flavor of that coffee," Perry added. 3. Water matters more than you think For homes with hard water, mineral buildup can gradually affect the machine's performance and, ultimately, the taste of home-brewed coffee. Perry suggested using faucets and showerheads as an easy visual cue. When they need cleaning, your coffee maker probably does, too. "Whatever you see in your sink faucets, your showerheads — that’s what’s happening with your coffee brewer," she said. LOOKING FOR BETTER COFFEE? HUNDREDS OF CHEFS AND SOMMELIERS SAY THESE ARE THE WORLD'S BEST The easiest way to limit that is to make sure you’re starting with good water, she added. She recommended water filtered at home or, in areas with particularly hard tap water, bottled water, and she cautioned against distilled or reverse-osmosis water, which lacks the minerals that help flavor coffee. Since "coffee [is] 98% water, you want good water, and you want it to have enough minerals because that’s what the coffee flavor sticks to," she said. 4. Coffee oils can build up in your grinder, too If you're grinding your own beans, the grinder doesn't need constant deep cleaning, but Perry does recommend checking the hopper and grounds area for an oily film. "I would absolutely make sure you’re wiping that out with a dry paper towel. Get the coffee oils off of it," she said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER A smell should also tip you off. "It’s not that fresh coffee smell, it’s that old coffee smell," she said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Perry added, "If you start to see coffee oils forming, the longer they stay, the harder they are to get off." 5. Don't bother putting coffee in the fridge The fridge is not the best spot to keep coffee grounds because they can absorb moisture and surrounding odors, according to Perry. "Your freezer is actually a better preservative," she said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES But even that might not be necessary. "Leave the one bag out that you’re using right now. As long as you’re consuming it within a month, it’s going to be fine," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Perry said the most important factors are the coffee itself and the water. She summed it up this way: "Start with really good ingredients… Coffee and water are absolutely going to be your two biggest starting points."

articles.title: Smartwatch AFib alert sends dad to ER before heart surgery
articles.summary: Joseph Holycross dismissed his racing heart for nearly two years until his Samsung Galaxy Watch detected atrial fibrillation and changed everything.
articles.body: When Joseph Holycross came home from work feeling off, he had plenty of reasons to brush it aside. He was a busy father of four, worked long hours and had grown accustomed to blaming a racing heart on caffeine and exhaustion. His wife, Jamie, saw something that worried her. She urged Joseph to use the ECG feature on his Samsung Galaxy Watch4 Classic. Seconds later, the result gave him a reason to stop making excuses and head to the emergency room. What doctors discovered would lead to a week in the hospital, open-heart surgery and new health concerns for Joseph's family. It also completely changed the way he looks at the smartwatch on his wrist. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed. Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist. Watch the free replays and get your checklists at CyberGuyLive.com CAN WEARABLES DETECT HEART PROBLEMS EARLY? DOCTOR BREAKS DOWN REAL DATA Joseph thought his racing heart had an explanation Joseph says the elevated heart rate had been happening on and off for roughly a year and a half to two years. At the time, just weeks before his 40th birthday, he did not see it as a warning sign. "I tend to fuel with caffeine. I'm a father of four, so, you know, we tend to drink coffee and things like that when we're tired to kind of push through the day," Joseph told CyberGuy. That made the symptoms easier to explain away. If his heart was racing, Joseph could point to coffee, exercise or a long day and keep going. Then Jamie noticed something different. "She had made the comment that I looked like I was short of breath, like I was breathing strangely," Joseph recalled. Jamie works as a respiratory therapist, so her concern carried weight. This time, Joseph agreed to check his heart with the ECG feature on his Samsung Galaxy Watch4 Classic. His Galaxy Watch showed AFib Joseph had owned his Galaxy Watch4 Classic for about three years. Before this happened, health monitoring was hardly the reason he wore it. He mainly liked being able to receive messages or answer calls while he worked without carrying his phone around the shop. He had tried the ECG feature perhaps once about a year earlier, mostly to see what the watch could do. This time was different. Joseph scrolled to the ECG feature, tapped the option to record and followed the directions on the screen. He says the watch instructed him to remain still and keep his finger on the sensor while it recorded for about 30 seconds. "It came up and told me immediately at the top in bold letters, atrial fibrillation," Joseph said. His reaction was immediate too, but it was not fear. "Denial," Joseph said. "I just thought it had to be a malfunction. I wasn't even 40 yet." He wondered whether the watch could be wrong, especially because it was an older model. So he ran the ECG again and then repeated it several more times. Jamie was not interested in continuing to test it at home. Joseph recalls her telling him, "We need to go to the ER and have an actual EKG done just to make sure." AI MAY SPOT DEADLY HEART RISK IN A ROUTINE ECG The watch changed Joseph's mind about going to the ER When I asked Joseph whether he would have gone to the emergency room that day without the watch, he did not hesitate. "Nope," he said. That answer gets to the heart of this story. The Galaxy Watch did not determine everything that was happening inside Joseph's heart. It gave him information that made his symptoms much harder to dismiss. Joseph sent the watch's ECG recording to his phone and brought it with him to the hospital. He says an ER doctor reviewed the tracing and confirmed that he was in AFib. Jamie remembers being struck by how closely the watch's result resembled what doctors were seeing. "The doctor was kind of impressed that it actually even looked like the rhythm that it showed looked like atrial fib," she said. Joseph expected to get checked out. Instead, he stayed in the hospital for about a week while doctors worked to understand the problems affecting his heart. Then came another major turn. About 10 days later, Joseph says he returned for open-heart surgery. "They had several things on my heart that they had to repair," he said. Jamie says doctors warned them what could have happened For Jamie, the experience reinforced something she had already seen through her work in healthcare. Wearable health data can give people useful information, but they have to take concerning results seriously and seek professional medical care. She says doctors warned the couple about what Joseph could have faced had he continued attributing his symptoms to caffeine or exercise. "He probably would have had a stroke, heart attack, or both," Jamie said. The family also says one of Joseph's doctors told them that without medical intervention, he likely would not have lived to see 45. That warning carries additional weight because Joseph had not considered himself someone with serious health problems. He was still 39 when his watch recorded the AFib reading. "It can happen to anyone," Jamie said. She hopes their experience encourages people to learn what the health features on their devices can actually do instead of waiting until something feels wrong. Hospital monitors gave Jamie another reason to trust the data Jamie had another perspective during Joseph's hospital stay because of her medical background. She says they compared the heart rate information on Joseph's watch with the hospital equipment while he was being monitored. According to Jamie, the readings were sometimes within about one beat per minute of the hospital monitor. That does not make a smartwatch a replacement for hospital equipment, but seeing the numbers track so closely left an impression on both of them. "I would definitely encourage people to take it seriously for sure," Jamie said. She views the watch as a tool that can give someone a reason to seek a professional opinion rather than something that should make medical decisions for them. Doctors raised concerns for Joseph's children and siblings Joseph's medical journey also created new questions for the rest of his family. He says doctors told him that some of the problems involving his heart could have a genetic component and that some may have been present since birth before gradually becoming more noticeable. That prompted doctors to recommend additional screening within the family. Joseph says his siblings have been encouraged to get checked for the same issues. His children will also need to undergo screening when they are adults. "It brought up a lot of concern," Joseph said. For a father of four, the discovery suddenly extended beyond his own recovery. The medical information doctors uncovered could potentially help his siblings and children watch for similar problems earlier. What the Samsung Galaxy Watch ECG can tell you Samsung says the ECG feature in its Samsung Health Monitor app records the electrical activity of the heart using a compatible Galaxy Watch. The recording takes about 30 seconds. Depending on the recording, Samsung says the app can return results including sinus rhythm, atrial fibrillation, high heart rate, AFib with a high heart rate, an inconclusive result or a poor recording. Samsung says an AFib result means the watch detected an irregular rhythm during the recording and advises users who receive that result to contact their doctor for guidance. Anyone who receives an AFib result with a high heart rate should contact a doctor as soon as possible. However, Samsung also cautions that its ECG feature does not replace traditional methods of diagnosis or treatment. Users should not interpret the device's output or take clinical action based on it without consulting a qualified healthcare professional. That difference is important in Joseph's case. His watch gave him an AFib result. Medical professionals then evaluated him and determined what treatment he needed. How to take an ECG on a compatible Galaxy Watch On Samsung's current software, the ECG feature works through the Samsung Health Monitor app on compatible Galaxy Watches paired with a compatible Galaxy phone. Availability and requirements can vary by device and region. To record an ECG, Samsung says to wear the watch snugly and rest your forearms comfortably on a table. Open Samsung Health Monitor on the watch and select ECG. Lightly rest a finger from your opposite hand on the watch's top button without pressing it, remain still and avoid talking while the watch records for 30 seconds. For the best reading, Samsung recommends sitting still beforehand, making sure the sensor is clean and dry and wearing the watch snugly so it lies flat against your wrist. Movement or poor skin contact can lead to a poor recording. Once the recording finishes, the result appears on the watch and can sync to the Samsung Health Monitor app on the paired phone. You can then review your ECG history and share a report with a healthcare professional. If you have symptoms that could indicate a medical emergency, do not wait for a smartwatch result before seeking emergency care. For Joseph, the watch now brings peace of mind After open-heart surgery, every strange feeling can carry more weight than it did before. Joseph described how even a small pain can make him wonder whether something is wrong again. Being able to check his heart rate and rhythm does not eliminate that concern, but he says it gives him reassurance. "You don't have to sit and worry, 'Oh, am I in AFib again?'" Joseph said. "I can check and, you know, it's a reliable source. It kind of puts you at peace." He has also been using the watch during his recovery to track his walking, steps and exercise. Before his medical ordeal, many of those health tools went unused. Now Joseph says the watch leaves his wrist mainly when he needs to charge it. "It's really been a peace of mind type" of device, Joseph said. Jamie hopes people learn what their watches can do Jamie says one of the lessons she wants other people to take away is surprisingly simple: If you already own a smartwatch with health features, learn how to use them. She sees people, including some who work in healthcare, use smartwatches primarily for steps or everyday notifications while ignoring other available tools. "I think the reassurance it gives people is amazing for anyone who even has, you know, cardiac issues," Jamie said. Joseph agrees. Before this happened, he knew his watch had additional capabilities, but he had little reason to explore them. Now he wants people to understand what may already be sitting on their wrists. "You've got to know that it's a lot more than just a watch," he said. For Joseph, that lesson became deeply personal. The watch did not perform his surgery or replace the doctors who diagnosed and treated him. What it did was give a busy 39-year-old father information that finally persuaded him to stop explaining away how he felt and head to the hospital. Kurt's key takeaways What stays with me about Joseph's story is that he came incredibly close to doing what many of us have done at one time or another: convincing himself there was a perfectly reasonable explanation for feeling off. He was working hard, drinking caffeine and raising four kids. A racing heart fit easily into the story he was already telling himself. Jamie noticed something different and pushed him to check. Then the watch gave Joseph a result he could no longer comfortably ignore. That combination ultimately got him through the doors of an emergency room. No smartwatch can tell you that you are healthy, and a reassuring reading should never override symptoms that concern you. Samsung makes that limitation clear. But Joseph's experience shows why the information these devices collect can be useful when it prompts someone to pay closer attention and talk to a healthcare professional. There is also a powerful family piece to his story. What doctors discovered led to new screening concerns for Joseph's siblings and, eventually, his children. A health scare that started with a 30-second reading on his wrist may now give other members of his family an opportunity to ask questions earlier. If your smartwatch warned you about a possible health problem but you felt fine, would you head to the doctor or be tempted to dismiss the alert? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com Sign up for my FREE CyberGuy Report CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Copyright 2026 CyberGuy.com. All rights reserved.

articles.title: Is It Healthy to Eat Nuts Every Day? Yes, If You Avoid These 3 Things, Dietitians Say
articles.summary: Nuts are delicious, but is it healthy to eat them every day? Dietitians share what to keep in mind if you eat nuts daily and the healthiest types.
articles.body: Nuts are one of the most popular snack foods, and for good reason. They’re delicious, nutrient-dense and portable. Plus, there’s dozens of varieties to choose from. Botanically, nuts are considered dry fruits that are enclosed in a hard shell with a protective husk, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Nuts have an exceptionally high fat content and tend to be higher in calories, which is why they can sometimes get a bad rap. “I think over time that has given the nuts this label. Just because they’re energy-dense doesn’t make them inherently unhealthy. They are also very nutrient dense,” Shannon Stockero, dietitian and spokesperson for The Obesity Society, tells TODAY.com. “Nuts are one food that most Americans could afford to prioritize or include more of in their diet,” says Stockero. That’s because nuts offer a range of impressive health benefits. Benefits of Nuts Nuts are little nutritional powerhouses. They’re rich in healthy, unsaturated fats, which are beneficial for heart and brain health, Stockero notes. The polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fats in nuts can also help lower bad cholesterol. Nuts are a good source of plant-based protein, offering around 4–6 grams per serving, says Natalie Rizzo, registered dietitian and TODAY.com nutrition editor. They’re also rich in fiber, which is important for gut health, Stockero adds. The trifecta of fats, protein and fiber in nuts helps with fullness, provides steady energy and makes meals and snacks more satisfying, Rizzo explains. “Replacing foods high in sources of unsaturated fats, like nuts, can help improve cholesterol levels and support cardiovascular health,” Rizzo explains. Nuts are also rich in vitamins, minerals and antioxidants, although the exact nutrients vary by type, Rizzo notes. For example, almonds are high in vitamin E, and Brazil nuts are packed with selenium. There aren’t many downsides to eating nuts. However, nuts are one of the top food allergens in the U.S. “Nut allergies can be very serious, so that’s something to be aware of,” Rizzo adds. Is It Healthy to Eat Nuts Every Day? Yes, you can enjoy nuts daily, the experts say. “A serving of nuts every day can be part of a very healthy diet,” says Rizzo. Routinely eating nuts provides you with a consistent intake of unsaturated fats, protein, vitamins minerals and antioxidants, says Stockero. The habit may also protect your health. In a 2022 study published in Advances in Nutrition, researchers found that eating 28 grams of nuts per day was associated with a lower risk of heart disease and death from all causes. No matter what time of day, nuts are a healthy choice. “I like them as a snack because the combination of protein, fiber and healthy fat keeps me satisfied between meals,” says Rizzo. Nuts can also boost the nutrient content of any meal. Sprinkle the nuts onto yogurt or oatmeal, use them as a garnish for salads and grain bowls or add them to baked goods. If you’re eating nuts every day, the dietitians recommend keeping a few things in mind: Pay Attention to Portion Size “A good general serving for nuts is about one ounce (28 grams), or a small handful,” says Rizzo. The exact number of nuts per serving varies depending on the type, Rizzo adds — 23 almonds, 18 cashews or 14 walnut halves, for example. “You don’t have to count out every nut you eat,” says Rizzo — just try to stick to about one ounce. A small portion of nuts contains quite a few calories, so if you’re eating several large handfuls, those add up quickly, Rizzo notes. “That doesn’t make nuts ‘fattening’ or something to avoid, but you do want to be mindful of portions, especially when you’re eating straight from a large container,” says Rizzo. Sticking to the portion size can ensure you’re getting the benefits from nuts without dramatically increasing your calorie intake, Stockero adds. It can be easy to overeat nuts from a large jar or bag. That’s why Stockero recommends opting for individual packs of nuts with one serving size or pre-portioning the nuts yourself. Opt for Unsalted If you’re eating nuts regularly, consider opting for unsalted varieties. “For an everyday option, I recommend raw or dry-roasted nuts with minimal added ingredients,” says Rizzo. That’s because salted nuts can be very high in sodium, which most Americans should be trying to cut back on. “Nuts are one food that can quickly add up in the sodium category,” says Stockero. Honey-roasted or candied nut also contain a lot of added sugar, Rizzo adds. If salted or seasoned nuts are the only kind you enjoy, it’s OK to eat them in moderation. However, Rizzo recommends being mindful of the ingredients, and choosing nuts with the least sodium, sugar and additives. Switch Up Your Nuts If you want to reap the health benefits of nuts, switch up the type you’re eating on a daily basis, the experts note. All nuts provide healthy fats, protein and fiber — but adding variety allows you to get different micronutrients, Stockero notes. Each nut is packed with a unique mix of vitamins, minerals and antioxidants. “Maybe one day you have walnuts in your oatmeal, and the next day, you put almonds in your yogurt,” says Stockero. Mixed nut blends are another easy way to get a variety of flavors, textures and nutrients. The Healthiest Nuts to Eat Daily All nuts are healthy options, but some offer a little more bang for your buck in the nutrient department. These nuts stand out for their impressive protein and micronutrients, according to the experts: Almonds One of the most widely consumed nuts in the world, almonds are loaded with plant protein and other nutrients. They’re among the highest-protein nuts you can eat, packing about 6 grams per serving. You’ll also get about 4 grams of dietary fiber to support gut health. One ounce of almonds provides about 20% of the daily value of vitamin E, which acts as an antioxidant to fight inflammation. “Almonds also have a good serving of calcium to support our bone health and immune system,” says Stockero. Walnuts Walnuts are also one of the healthiest nuts you can eat, says Stockero. One serving of walnuts offers about 4 grams of protein and 2 grams of fiber, but they really stand out for their other nutrients. “Walnuts are very high in plant-based omega-3 fatty acids, including alphalinolic acid (ALA), which can help lower systemic inflammation and support brain health,” says Stockero. You’ll also get folate, an essential B vitamin, along with vitamin E an some magnesium. Pistachios These bright green nuts are another great option, says Stockero. Pistachios pack about 6 grams of protein per serving along with 3 grams of gut-healthy fiber, which helps with satiety and curbing hunger. “They also tend to be lower in calories because they’re a little bit lower in fat,” says Stockero. Pistachios also provide antioxidants, such as lutein, which can support eye health and cognitive function, the experts note. Brazil Nuts Brazil nuts are another top choice among dietitians for daily consumption. They’re loaded with heart-healthy unsaturated fats and provide about 4 grams of plant protein per serving. But Brazil nuts really stand out for their micronutrients. Just two nuts contain over 300% of the daily value of selenium, an essential trace mineral that helps with thyroid function and immune support. One serving of Brazil nuts provides about 25% of the daily value of magnesium, which supports nerve and muscle function. Plus, they contain some iron, copper and manganese. Peanuts Peanuts are technically a legume, but they’re a nut in the culinary sense — and deserve an honorable mention. They’re loaded with filling protein and healthy fats, which can keep you satiated between meals. One ounce of peanuts provides about 7 grams of plant protein, plus a hefty dose of healthy unsaturated fats. Peanuts are also rich in B vitamins, which play a big role in energy metabolism, says Stockero.

articles.title: ‘Addiction Economy’ is a bad gamble for young men. Here’s their way out
articles.summary: Roughly 35% of young men gamble daily or weekly as the "Addiction Economy" exploits their isolation. But their ambitions reveal a path forward.
articles.body: You cannot scroll on social media, watch television or even make a purchase online without being inundated with advertisements for sports gambling and prediction markets. Companies are spending millions to make sure we see them, and their primary target audience is young men. Data from the Institute for Family Studies confirms just how deeply this has taken hold: roughly one-third (35%) of young men gamble daily or weekly. This is not the only digital habit growing among young men today. Nearly half (42%) watch pornography daily or weekly, and most young men (86%) play video games daily or weekly. This is what some people refer to as the "addiction economy." As a pastor, I know young men who engage in these things every day. And, to be honest, I’m not surprised. More than half (61%) of young men say they often feel they have little control over the things happening to them. Coping with this pervasive felt lack of agency drives them toward digital escapes that offer a temporary illusion of control, thrill or connection. DAVID MARCUS: BRAVE NEW WORLD OF PREDICTION MARKETS CAN MAKE US ALL INSIDE TRADERS Yet, we know two crucial things about today’s young men: they’re ambitious — and they’re vulnerable. An overwhelming majority (84%) of young men say they have ambitious plans for their future. They want to grow. They want to succeed, and in some sense feel that they’re capable of doing so. But they’re also profoundly isolated and frustrated. They’re facing a world where the paths to traditional success — like career success, homeownership, marriage, children and more — feel washed away or blocked. They struggle with the ability to make friends with other young men or relate to young women. AI IS CHANGING MODERN DATING, BUT EXPERTS WARN IT'S MAKING PEOPLE 'RELATIONALLY STUPID' The addiction economy demands young men’s attention, time and money, and undermines their vision for a successful life. Left unchecked, society and commercial forces will continue to exploit or ignore their tendency at early ages to use things to numb pain, deal with anxiety, or cope with discouragement. But the true role of society should be to help them fulfill their aspirations for good and build lives of purpose. If we don’t offer them a better vision for their lives, the addiction economy will gladly fill the void. Older generations are quick to notice and criticize young men for retreating into digital vices, but scolding and shaming have never produced excellence. Young men may be demoralized, but they haven’t given up. What they need is a guide and a path forward. They need to know they can build a life they actually want and can inhabit. POLL FINDS SHARP RISE IN YOUNG MEN CALLING RELIGION 'VERY IMPORTANT' Young men need formation and support if they are to develop their open-ended sense of potential and ambition into real success and healthy relationships with peers, colleagues and romantic partners. They are capable of building good and desirable lives for themselves, and of attaining real excellence. But they need help to do so. And any invested, stable adult is capable of providing the support they need. Their needs are ultimately simple, though urgent. So, go out of your way to establish strong, authentic, transparent relationships with the young men in your life. Show them they’re not alone, that they’re not unique in their struggles. Provide relatability and accountability, hand in hand. These relationships will help remove the burden of guilt, of embarrassment, of shame for young men. This is part of being a human. We’re all going to struggle, often with the same things. These common struggles allow us to encourage and remind young men that they have the ability to overcome them. DADS AREN’T OPTIONAL — AND AMERICA’S KIDS ARE PAYING THE BRUTAL PRICE It’s also important to help young men feel like they have agency in their own lives, and that their lives have meaning. They have a lot of questions: how to be successful, find a fulfilling job, make friends and navigate dating. Often, we have to help them find answers and take practical steps to feel more in control of their future. Make sure they have the space they need to ask important questions and share vulnerable feelings or experiences, without feeling judged, dismissed or doubted. Young men also need a clear vision for their lives, and a clear vision of how they fit into their own communities. Help them develop their ambitions into specific plans. Help them come to know and understand how much impact they can have, just by showing up to serve. Whether at work, at church, in their friendships or in their families, young men need opportunities to contribute, make a difference and see that their lives matter to the people around them. I WORRY LESS ABOUT SCREENS THAN ABOUT THE CHALLENGES TODAY’S TEENS NEVER FACE We as their mentors have to help them build lives they want to live. And in order to help them build those lives, we must step into their present lives without fear, without judgment and without hesitation. They want to succeed — they just need our support. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The addiction economy that has them firmly in its grasp isn’t something to be feared. It is one of the most profound opportunities for us to enter and help change the course of the lives of young men. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It’s time we stepped in.

articles.title: 10-minute fitness habit can help adults over 40 maintain muscle and stay strong
articles.summary: CEO Carl Daikeler compares metabolism to a furnace: Muscle is the coal and cardio stokes it, urging a balance of strength training and cardiovascular work.
articles.body: Adults over 40 may not need to spend hours in the gym to maintain muscle, preserve mobility and stay strong. According to Los Angeles fitness entrepreneur Carl Daikeler, just 10 minutes of targeted resistance exercise each day can help preserve muscle, mobility and long-term function. Daikeler, 63, who has spent 28 years leading BODi, the fitness brand formerly known as Beachbody, says his approach to exercise stems from a practical desire to stay healthy without having to be a dedicated fitness enthusiast. 4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS "I don't like to eat healthy, I don't like to work out," Daikeler told Fox News Digital at the Strong New York conference in September. "I'm just constantly trying to figure out how I can hack my way without having to overturn my life to become one of these diehard health and fitness people, because I'm never going to become that." For adults looking to stay healthy in midlife, Daikeler recommends what he considers a "minimum effective dose" — short, targeted resistance workouts at home instead of lengthy gym sessions. "Ten minutes a day, and you can establish and build and maintain muscle," he said. WANT TO AGE BETTER? RESEARCHERS SAY 4-MINUTE ROUTINE MAY HELP PREVENT DANGEROUS FALLS Federal physical activity guidelines say that adults should perform muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups at least two days per week, in addition to regular aerobic activity. Rather than doing a full-body workout every day, Daikeler recommends rotating muscle groups — focusing on the chest one day, upper body the next, then legs and glutes — to build consistency without requiring lengthy gym sessions. "Ten minutes a day, and you can establish and build and maintain muscle." "Do that consistently, and you're going to find your strength return, your muscles return, your joints will start to respond appropriately," he said. The 10-minute approach can be especially valuable for people taking GLP-1 medications, who may be trying to preserve muscle mass and bone density while losing weight but may feel intimidated by traditional gyms, Daikeler said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES For individuals seeking more significant weight loss, he recommends extending daily activity to 20 or 30 minutes, incorporating a balance of strength training and cardiovascular exercise. The balancing act Daikeler cautioned against focusing exclusively on either cardio or resistance training, noting that different exercise types serve distinct functions in the body. "Your body's like a furnace," Daikeler said. "The coal in that furnace is muscle. So you want to build muscle. But then you want to stoke that coal, and that's cardio. So, you need a balance of both things." While resistance training builds muscle and strengthens bones and connective tissue, cardiovascular exercise challenges the heart and lungs, helping to maintain overall fitness, he said. Shifting focus to function As adults age, Daikeler says the primary motivation for maintaining physical activity should shift away from aesthetic goals and toward functional mobility and independence. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Reflecting on his personal experience visiting his father in an assisted living facility, Daikeler observed how residents struggled with basic movement and balance. Many residents relied on walkers and canes, and often stopped walking before talking to one another because they feared tripping over cracks in the pavement, he recalled. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "This is no longer about my abs," Daikeler added. "I need to work out in order to be able to walk and talk at the same time into my 90s ... It's no longer about aesthetics and vanity. It's really about mobility." Maintaining healthy physical habits means accepting daily short-term discomfort to protect long-term independence, Daikeler noted. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If I do 20 minutes of discomfort, the rest of the day is awesome," he said, adding that the goal is to consistently incorporate resistance training, cardio and flexibility work into a daily routine.

articles.title: DR MARC SIEGEL: The angels behind Alcoholics Anonymous still inspire hope
articles.summary: Middle-aged adults are drinking more and dying at alarming rates from alcohol use disorder, but a faith-based cure from the 1930s still works.
articles.body: Alcohol is still something to be worried about. Granted, national data shows a decline coming out of the pandemic, but the overall numbers are still higher than they were in 2018. Not only that, but though Gen Zers and millennials are drinking less, middle-aged adults are drinking more, with an increase in heavy drinking since 2018. Some of this is because middle-aged adults face increased pressures as they try to manage both aging parents and children who are in adolescence or early adulthood and are just finding themselves. But though drinking may temporarily ease stress, the long-term health risks are significant. A recent study from Colorado determined that older adults are more likely to drink alone, which carries with it additional health risks, including cognitive decline. There are an estimated 28 million Americans who suffer from alcohol use disorder, with a substantial portion of them being middle-aged. Not only that, but about 50% of the deaths due to alcohol in the U.S. occur among middle-aged adults. HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK Faith-based cures remain highly effective for alcoholism, with none more effective than Alcoholics Anonymous, which was developed in the 1930s by Bill Wilson and Dr. Bob Smith after a chance meeting, the kind that the famed psychiatrist Carl Jung called synchronicity, or meaningful coincidence. They became messengers of God for each other and ultimately, for millions of other alcoholics with their 12-step program based largely on making a spiritual connection. In my new book, "The Angels Among Us," I devote a chapter to the miracle recovery of Bill Wilson and his consequential friendship with Dr. Bob. Bill is admitted to Towns Hospital in New York City in 1934 for the fourth time because of alcohol intoxication followed by withdrawal. He is in the depths of despair and is not sure if he will survive. And then he experiences the central miracle of his life as he demands that God show Himself. CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND "The room lights up with a blinding glare of light. Wilson is seized by an ecstasy he has never known. He stands on a mountaintop with a great wind blowing. He thinks to himself, 'This is not a wind of air. This is spirit. This is the God of the preachers.' "Bill feels that a great, clean strength is blowing through him, that he is now free." Bill Wilson tells about his experience to his medical angel, Dr. Silkworth, who is tending to him there in the hospital, who decides he is not crazy, but that a great psychic event has occurred. This changes Bill's life, as the doctor/"angel" advises him to hang on to this experience and to share it. By meeting other alcoholics where they live, and not speaking down to them, by not preaching, Wilson and later Dr. Bob spread faith, goodwill, and ultimately sobriety. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION In today's world, this lesson remains crucial. It is the in-person exchange of peer-to-peer kindness and caring that gives us all the chance to heal. It doesn't work the same way on social media, and self-destructive behavior (including alcohol addiction) is much more likely to occur in isolation. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There is still a lesson to be learned from Bill Wilson's experience. Doctors can be angels of healing, just as fellow sufferers can. articles.title: In 2010, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and his wife gave $100 million to UCSF; five years later, its new San Francisco children's hospital opened with 183 beds and a rooftop helipad
articles.summary: In 2010, Salesforce co-founder and CEO Marc Benioff and his wife, Lynne Benioff, donated $100 million to the University of California, San Francisco
articles.body: In 2010, Salesforce co-founder and CEO Marc Benioff and his wife, Lynne Benioff, donated $100 million to the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) to help fund the construction of a new children's hospital, a project that would later become one of the most significant healthcare developments in the San Francisco Bay Area. Announced in June 2010, the donation was described as the largest gift ever made mainly to the UCSF Children's Hospital. Also, it is one of the largest private donations made to a children’s hospital in the United States at that time. As part of the recognition and gratitude towards the contribution, the facility also renamed the facility as UCSF Benioff Children's Hospital. As per UCSF, the gift made by Benioff supported the development of a new children’s hospital at the Mission Bay campus in San Francisco. The facility was designed with 183 beds specifically for children and their families, with expanded capacity compared with the existing hospital and an on-site helipad to accommodate critically ill patients requiring emergency transport.Hospital opens five years laterFive years after the gift was announced, the new UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital San Francisco opened as part of a larger 289-bed hospital complex at Mission Bay. UCSF said the hospital began operations on 1 February 2015 and featured 183 beds, increasing capacity from the previous facility while providing specialised care environments designed for children and their families.One of the hospital’s key features was a rooftop helipad that allowed critically ill newborns, children and pregnant women to be transported directly from community hospitals across Northern California. The facility also included a dedicated paediatric emergency department and intensive care services designed specifically for young patientsSecond $100 million commitmentBefore the opening of the hospital, the Benioffs also announced another donation of $100 million in 2014 in order to support USCF Benioff Children’s Hospital and its affiliate, Children’s Hospital & Research Center Oakland. The funding was also intended to strengthen paediatric research, clinical programmes and talent recruitment across both institutions. After the affliction, the hospitals were also renamed as UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital San Francisco and UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland.Focus on family-centred careAs per SUCF, the Mission Bay hospital was designed mainly around the needs and requirements of children and their families. The rooms of the patients were built to accommodate the parents who were staying with their children, while the additional rehabilitation, play therapy and outdoor spaces were included to support recovery. Along with this, UCSF also highlighted that the hospital’s proximity to its biomedical research campus, which was intended to speed the translation of scientific discoveries into clinical treatments.The project remains one of the most prominent examples of healthcare philanthropy by a Silicon Valley executive, helping create a major paediatric care and research hub serving patients across the Bay Area and beyond.You use AI every day. articles.title: Medieval leprosy hospital uncovered in Lincoln
articles.summary: Walls at the site have been unearthed as part of a three-day dig by Time Team experts.
articles.body:
The walls of what is thought to be one of medieval England's earliest and largest leprosy hospitals have been uncovered in Lincoln by Time Team archaeologists.

A three-day dig started on Friday on the South Common at the site of the Hospital of the Holy Innocents, which housed up to 20 people with leprosy around the late 11th to early 12th Centuries.

Time Team's Prof Carenza Lewis said they had found traces of square features where it is thought people were housed, which "haven't been excavated before, anywhere".

The dig marks the beginning of a three-year project backed by the National Lottery Heritage Fund.

The remains of the building were found last year during a Local Landscapes and Hidden Histories project.

More than 100 volunteers were involved in excavating test pits which uncovered what were thought to be the medieval boundary walls of the hospital.

Time Team carried out a geophysical survey of the area, like an X-ray of the ground, and volunteers have dug a 30m-long (98ft) trench to join up the two test pits where traces of the walls were found.

Lewis said a wall runs all the way down the trench and either side of it, according to the survey.

"We know from historical documents that there were up to 20 lepers housed here, and we know that they had little sorts of curtilages… which implies they're separate little buildings, little houses with a little yard, perhaps," she explained.

"What we've got all along this wall here are traces of little square features, about 5m (16ft) across, that are big enough to be a little building or a yard area, and we've got lots of them."

City of Lincoln Council said it believed the hospital remained in use for about five centuries.

The Hidden Histories Unearthed project, supported by £248,139 from the National Lottery Heritage Fund and led by Anglia Ruskin University, aims to uncover more about the people who lived and died at the hospital.

"You'd need to have resources to get in here," Lewis said.

"If you had enough money and could buy your way into a leper hospital, it's a bit like getting a place in a private care home or something like that."

The council said local residents would have opportunities to get involved in further archaeological excavations and activities as the project continues.

articles.title: Newlywed from Kollam alleges brutal torture by husband, police register dowry harassment case
articles.summary: Kollam newlywed alleges brutal torture and dowry harassment by husband in Saudi Arabia; Chavara police book husband and parents under Dowry Prohibition Act.
articles.body: Kollam: A 24-year-old newlywed from Neendakara in Kollam has alleged that her husband subjected her to brutal physical and mental torture in Saudi Arabia, including hitting her head with a pressure cooker, kicking her lower abdomen and hitting her private parts, after harassing her over dowry.The woman, who returned to Kerala on Sept 30, is undergoing treatment at Kollam District Hospital with multiple injury marks and bruises on her body. Chavara police have registered a case against her husband Nandu, 28, and his parents Dinesh and Jagadamma on her complaint. The case has been registered under Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act.According to her complaint, the harassment began within a week of her marriage on July 27. Her husband’s family allegedly complained that she had brought insufficient dowry and repeatedly taunted her over the amount given by her parents.She alleged that the harassment was not confined to demands for dowry. Nandu allegedly compared her with his ex-girlfriend and told her that she was not good-looking enough or suitable for his social status. He allegedly restricted her communication with her friends, changed her phone number and prevented her from freely using WhatsApp and social media accounts.About a month after the marriage, Nandu went to Saudi Arabia for work. She alleged that he continued to verbally abuse and control her through phone and video calls. Following the harassment, she returned to her parental home.Nandu later took her to Saudi Arabia, telling her that she could stay with him until she found a job and that they could spend time together. She said the situation became much worse after she reached Saudi. The couple was staying alone in a flat where Nandu allegedly began physically assaulting her repeatedly. She alleged that he used whatever was available in the house to attack her.She alleged that she suffered a head injury after Nandu struck her with a pressure cooker. She also alleged that he kicked her in the lower abdomen and hit her on her private parts. She claimed that her body bore around 30 injury marks and that several parts had turned blue because of severe bruising.“I had told the police about all these things when they came to record my statement, but none of them was documented,” she said.She also alleged that Nandu would hold a knife against her and threaten to stab her, while forcing her to make audio recordings containing false and humiliating statements about herself. She said she was forced to say in the recordings that she had sexual relationship with several men before and after her marriage and had uploaded intimate material on pornographic websites. She was also allegedly forced to say that she wanted to work in a sex racket after divorcing Nandu. “He sent those recordings to my family and people in my locality. Everyone believed them,” she said.She said Nandu also allegedly took control of the money in her bank account. “He behaved like a psychopath. His family knew about the harassment,” she added.After noticing the recordings, her parents contacted Nandu and informed him that they did not want the relationship to continue and wanted their daughter to return to Kerala. She subsequently returned on Sept 30 and was admitted to District Hospital. Her family and hospital authorities informed the police, following which officers recorded her statement and registered the case.Police said Nandu is currently in Saudi Arabia and the investigation is under way. The woman is a postgraduate in data analytics.Stay updated with the latest Thiruvananthapuram news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Suicide pact whiff in deaths of elderly couple at Panchasayar flat
articles.summary: Elderly couple found dead in Panchasayar flat: man hanging, wife on bed after recent stroke. Police probe suicide pact, murder-suicide; note, Rs 1 lakh found.
articles.body: Kolkata: A couple in their 60s, who had lost their son years ago and were dealing with the woman’s recent stroke, were found dead inside their Panchasayar flat on Sunday morning.Police said Asit Ash (66) was found hanging from the ceiling while his wife Mandira Ash (64) was lying unconscious on the bed when officers broke open the door of their ground-floor flat. They were taken to NRS Medical College and Hospital, where doctors declared them dead on arrival.Mandira had suffered a stroke a few days ago and was undergoing treatment at SSKM Hospital. She returned home about two days ago but had not been keeping well, police said.Officers said neither appeared to have external injury marks. “We have sent the bodies for post-mortem, but prima facie it seems to be a case of suicide,” an officer said.Police are examining two possibilities. “One is that the husband may have killed his wife and then committed suicide. The other is that the woman died and the husband took his life after that,” the officer said.Police learnt from relatives and residents that the couple had a son who died of kidney failure. A resident of the five-storey apartment said the couple earlier lived in Howrah’s Balitikuri, where Asit ran a lathe machine business. They moved to Panchasayar about a decade ago following their son’s death.Their daughter and son-in-law also live in the neighbourhood, residents said.Mandira’s sister, who lives in the same building, called the couple on Sunday morning. When no one answered, she went to their flat and found the door locked from inside. After repeated knocking failed to elicit a response, police were informed at 9.18 am.“A team went there and broke open the door to find the man hanging and the woman lying unconscious on the bed,” said an officer of Panchasayar PS.Residents told police they had heard sounds from the couple’s flat till around 10.30 pm on Saturday. Neighbours said the couple did not appear to be under financial stress. They also claimed a suicide note and Rs 1 lakh were found in the flat. “They wrote in the note that the money was meant for their final rites and that no one should have to bear the expenses,” a neighbour said.The couple had been living for several years in the ground-floor flat of a building at Naba Malancha, Nayabad, under Panchasayar police station.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolkata | Silver Rate in Kolkata | Bank Holidays in Kolkata | Public Holidays in Kolkata | Kolkata AQI | Weather in Kolkata | Petrol Price in Kolkata | Diesel Price in Kolkata | CNG Price in Kolkata | LPG Price in KolkataStay updated with the latest Kolkata news. articles.title: Unwilling to wait for ‘Thaimaaman gold ring,’ man assaults village health nurse, kin
articles.summary: Village health nurse and two relatives attacked in Kumbakonam after man demanded Thaimaaman gold ring out of turn; police register case, injuries treated.
articles.body: Thanjavur: A village health nurse and two of her relatives were attacked by a man in Kumbakonam on Saturday after he picked up an argument over collecting a gold ring under the state govt’s new ‘Thaimaaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam.’ Police on Sunday registered a case against the man, based on a complaint from the nurse, R Alamelu.The scheme, launched by chief minister Joseph Vijay on Sept 28, entitles babies born between Jun 22 and Sept 28 to a one-gram gold ring. The state govt has been clearing the backlog by allotting parents specific time slots to collect the ring based on date-wise seniority.Madan of Muzhaiyur and his wife Vanitha had a baby boy at Kumbakonam govt hospital on Sept 16. Alamelu R, 35, the village health nurse at Patteeswaram primary health centre, had registered the birth. On Saturday afternoon, Madan visited the PHC and demanded the ring. When Alamelu told him that it would be issued only according to his allotted slot and asked him to leave, he picked up an argument.According to police, later in the evening, he turned up in an inebriated condition at Alamelu’s house and demanded the ring. He threw stones at the premises and allegedly abused her. On being alerted, her aunt B Sujatha and brother V Suman confronted him. Madan allegedly attacked all three with a spade and fled. The injured trio were admitted to Kumbakonam GH for treatment.“I explained to the beneficiary Madan that there is a cap on how many people can be given the rings each day. But he resorted to violence. When I went to Patteeswaram police station to register a complaint, the cops asked me to get admitted at the GH. It was only on Sunday afternoon that they registered the case after we were admitted to the GH,” Alamelu said.Doctors said the distribution responsibility should be given to the social welfare department. “Since the gold is stored in govt hospitals, we have to take care of its security. With staffing shortages and high case volumes, managing physical gold distribution at the time of patient discharge adds heavy clerical and administrative stress,” said Dr T Aruleeswaran, treasurer of the service doctors and PG association.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Trichy | Silver Rate in Trichy | Bank Holidays in Trichy | Public Holidays in TrichyStay updated with the latest Trichy news. articles.title: Subtle change in how you speak could be early sign of dementia risk, new research suggests
articles.summary: A new Drexel University study of 833,417 participants links voice disorders to a 58% higher likelihood of developing dementia or cognitive impairment.
articles.body: New research suggests that voice disorders, including shifts in vocal pitch, volume or clarity, could indicate a higher probability of developing dementia or cognitive impairment in the future. A study involving 833,417 participants aged 50 and older examined the connection between a voice disorder, hearing loss, or both with the chance of developing cognitive impairment or dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease, beginning a year after the voice disorder and hearing loss diagnoses. The findings from the study, conducted by a team at the Drexel University College of Medicine in Philadelphia, were published in the Journal of Voice. EVERYDAY TASK MAY HELP DETECT EARLY DEMENTIA SIGNS BEFORE DIAGNOSIS, STUDY FINDS Results showed that participants with a voice disorder but no hearing loss had a 58% increased likelihood of developing dementia or cognitive issues in the future — whereas participants with a voice disorder and hearing loss had a 104% chance. For all participants with voice disorders, with or without hearing loss, there was a 29% increased probability of developing dementia or cognitive impairment, whereas those with only hearing loss had a 27% greater risk. "We found the strongest link with dementia among patients experiencing a voice disorder and hearing loss," said Robert Sataloff, a professor and chair at the Drexel University College of Medicine, Science Alert reported. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Importantly, we found that those with a voice disorder and no hearing loss were at greater risk than patients who experience hearing loss only," he added. Examples of voice disorders include laryngitis, vocal cord paralysis, vocal cord lesions and spasmodic dysphonia (laryngeal dystonia), among others, according to the Cleveland Clinic. Regardless of the possible correlation between vocal issues and dementia, researchers noted that seeking treatment for a voice disorder could also benefit a patient’s brain. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Hearing loss and trouble speaking could discourage individuals from socializing with others, and studies have shown that social engagement can stimulate the brain and play a role in warding off dementia. Sataloff said that it’s "only natural" for voice disorders and hearing loss to be connected to cognitive impairment. Those who experience pain or discomfort when talking or singing might "participate less often in brain-supporting social or other engaging activities," he noted. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Despite the study's findings, having a voice disorder doesn’t necessarily mean that future cognitive impairment is absolutely certain. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Additionally, it’s not guaranteed that vocal issues indicate the beginning of a decline in brain function or the onset of dementia or Alzheimer’s.

articles.title: Elite CEOs pay $20K to endure a psychedelic 'hell ride' that rewires the human brain
articles.summary: Ibogaine clinics in Mexico charge up to $20,000 for psychedelic treatments that carry serious cardiac risks and potentially fatal complications.
articles.body: Americans are spending thousands of dollars to travel for ibogaine treatments despite warnings that the powerful psychedelic carries potentially dangerous and even deadly risks. Executives, entrepreneurs and other high-performing professionals are paying as much as $20,000 in search of a mental reset, addiction treatment or improved performance, according to the New York Post. At Ibogaine Clinic in Playa del Carmen, the center says it helps coordinate airport transfers, accommodations and other travel logistics for patients. DR. DREW PINSKY REVEALS RED FLAG IN PRESLEY GERBER ADDICTION TREATMENT BEFORE MODEL'S DEATH Other clinics have turned treatment into a multi-day retreat. At Beond Ibogaine in Cancún, programs include medically supervised care alongside lodging, yoga, meditation, massage and integration sessions, according to the center's website. With ibogaine unavailable for medical use in the United States, some Americans are traveling to Mexico to seek treatment. While Mexico has emerged as one of the leading destinations for ibogaine treatment, psychedelic retreats have also expanded elsewhere in Latin America, including Costa Rica, where travelers seek alternative wellness and recovery experiences, according to reports. Ibogaine drew renewed public attention following the death of Presley Gerber, the 27-year-old son of Cindy Crawford. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Gerber had traveled to Mexico for what he described as an "ibogaine flood," a high-dose treatment involving the psychoactive substance, while struggling with addiction, Fox News Digital previously reported. He had spoken publicly about turning to ibogaine in an effort to "rewire" his brain. Addiction specialist Dr. Drew Pinsky warned against viewing ibogaine or other alternative psychedelic treatments as a cure for substance-use disorder. "I've had patients using ibogaine or ayahuasca for decades, and there's nothing magic about it, I assure you," Pinsky told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES While some Americans travel to Mexico seeking relief from addiction, others are paying thousands of dollars for ibogaine experiences marketed as a way to improve performance, recover from burnout or gain a new perspective.
